title: Bivariate Data Analysis v1

findings.finding: The seedling questions require estimating between observations in both directions before this method is taught.
findings.breakdown: Earlier examples read existing plotted points. These parts require selecting surrounding observations and estimating an unrecorded height or time; reading an existing point does not supply that decision.
findings.checked: Checked all teaching preceding scatterplots and p6–p7 teaching, together with p8-q1 and p8-q2-a through d. None models estimation between observations. The interpolation teaching on p19 comes later.
findings.assumptions: Cartesian plotting and decimal arithmetic are prior knowledge. Calculator availability does not affect the finding.

repair.proposal: Before p8-q2-e, add: 'To estimate between observations, use the observations on either side and assume approximately steady growth over that short interval. At weeks 3 and 4, the heights are 9 cm and 10.5 cm. At week 3.5, estimate halfway between these heights: 9.75 cm. To estimate time from height, reverse the process: 14.35 cm is halfway between 13.5 cm at week 6 and 15.2 cm at week 7, so estimate 6.5 weeks.'

findings.doneWhen: Students see how to select surrounding observations and estimate between them in both directions before parts e and f.

findings.finding: Practice requires identifying and drawing perfect correlation, but preceding teaching supplies no criterion distinguishing it from strong correlation.
findings.breakdown: The definition of strong correlation also accommodates exactly collinear points. Students must choose between perfect and strong in p16-q3 and construct perfect correlations in p17-q6 without that distinction being taught.
findings.checked: Checked all preceding teaching, including p14 strength definitions and figures and p15 identification and key ideas. None defines perfect correlation. Practice answers are not preceding teaching.
findings.assumptions: Perfect correlation is new terminology here. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Append to p14-strength: 'Perfect positive or negative correlation: every point lies exactly on one rising or falling straight line. Strong but not perfect correlation: the points lie close to a straight line, with some scatter.'

findings.doneWhen: An explicit criterion distinguishes perfect correlation from strong correlation with scatter before p16-q3.

findings.finding: Use the carrot measurements to connect an individual exception with the overall positive correlation.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up uses an actual pair from the dataset to examine why positive correlation permits exceptions.
findings.checked: The 15 cm carrot has mass 19 g; the 14.5 cm carrot has mass 21 g. The differences are 0.5 cm and 2 g. Hedging and overall correlation have already been taught.
findings.assumptions: Only methods available by the end of this topic are required.

repair.proposal: After p17-q7-c add: d) How much longer is the 15 cm carrot than the 14.5 cm carrot? Answer: 0.5 cm. e) How much less does the 15 cm carrot weigh than the 14.5 cm carrot? Answer: 2 g. f) Does this pair prevent the overall correlation from being positive? Explain why. Answer: No; longer carrots generally have greater mass, although individual pairs can be exceptions.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up remains attached to the carrot question and distinguishes an overall trend from an individual exception.

findings.finding: Numerical extrapolation requires extending a fitted line after earlier teaching explicitly prohibits extension, without explaining when that restriction changes.
findings.breakdown: The p10 prohibition is reinforced by rejecting an otherwise suitable extended line. Although p19 introduces predictions outside the data and illustrates them, its guided question again discourages extension. Students receive conflicting instructions about the operation required later.
findings.checked: Checked p10-information-block, p10-appropriateness-c, all p19 teaching and the subsequent prediction practice. The later explicit instruction to extend in p23-q9-b supplies the operation but does not reconcile the earlier prohibition.
findings.assumptions: Students carry forward the explicit drawing convention. Calculator availability is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Add to p19-definition: 'When initially drawing the fitted line, keep it within the observed data range. To make an extrapolation, deliberately extend that same straight line beyond the observations and read from it as before. The prediction is less reliable because the relationship may change.'

findings.doneWhen: Students can distinguish the initial drawing convention from deliberately extending a line to make a cautious prediction.

findings.finding: Vary the gradient while holding the employee-age context and intercept fixed.
findings.breakdown: The sequence isolates how gradient magnitude and sign affect the interpreted rate of change.
findings.checked: Each interpretation follows from the gradient as change in predicted hours per additional year of age. The zero-gradient case follows from the same linear model.
findings.assumptions: These are alternative illustrative models, rather than additional fits asserted for the supplied observations.

repair.proposal: Extend p27-q2-b under its existing instruction, 'What does it represent?', with alternative equations: (i) y=0.022x+6.2658; (ii) y=0.044x+6.2658; (iii) y=0.088x+6.2658; (iv) y=−0.044x+6.2658. Add only this instruction: 'Predict how the interpretation changes before answering each part.' Expected answers: predicted hours increase by 0.022, 0.044 and 0.088 hours per additional year respectively; in (iv), they decrease by 0.044 hours per additional year. Follow with the unpatterned part (v) y=0x+6.2658. Answer: predicted hours do not change with age. Keep x as employee age in years and y as hours worked throughout.

findings.doneWhen: The added parts vary only gradient, retain the existing interpretation task and add only one prediction instruction.

findings.finding: The topic does not rehearse substitution or solving two-step linear equations before both are used directly in its introductory examples.
findings.breakdown: Students must substitute a contextual input, or subtract a constant and divide by a decimal coefficient, while also deciding which variable is supplied. The preceding topic rehearses identifying and interpreting coefficients rather than these algebraic operations.
findings.checked: Checked all preceding teaching and the supplied practice from the immediately preceding topic. The p25 review covers coefficient identification, graph reading and equation construction; p26 and p27 interpret gradients and intercepts. Neither rehearses the required substitution and equation-solving procedures.
findings.assumptions: Substitution and two-step equations are prior learning, consistent with the course library. A calculator is assumed for decimal arithmetic; product evaluation itself is not the missing review piece.

repair.proposal: Before p28-method add four short items: (a) Evaluate 1.4x+8 when x=15. (b) Evaluate −0.6d+24 when d=12. (c) Solve 38=1.5x+8. (d) Solve 19=1.1x−14. Answers: 29; 16.8; x=20; x=30. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse substitution and solving for an unknown input with decimal coefficients before the contextual examples.

findings.finding: The central scale category needs to describe little or no linear correlation rather than absence of any relationship.
findings.breakdown: Labelling the entire central interval 'No relationship' can teach that a small coefficient rules out every relationship. The earlier distinction between linear and nonlinear patterns does not explain that a nonlinear pattern can have a coefficient near zero.
findings.checked: Checked p14 linear and nonlinear association teaching, p15 key ideas and p33's definition of Pearson's r as a measure of linear association. The definition supplies the scope, but does not reconcile the scale's broader label. The supplied answer for r=0.23 appropriately says 'little or no linear relationship'.
findings.assumptions: The central label is 'No relationship' as quoted in the candidate; the supplied diagram specification lists its interval but does not transcribe that label. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Replace the central label with 'Little or no linear correlation' and add: 'A value close to zero indicates little linear association. A curved relationship may still be present, so check the scatterplot.'

findings.doneWhen: The scale and accompanying explanation consistently distinguish little linear association from absence of any relationship.

findings.finding: Use paired coefficients in the gym context to separate direction from strength.
findings.breakdown: Reordering the proposed coefficients makes each consecutive comparison change either sign or magnitude.
findings.checked: On the supplied scale, magnitudes 0.64, 0.90 and 0.38 are moderate, strong and weak respectively. Sign determines direction. No calculation of r is required.
findings.assumptions: The alternative coefficients use the same variables and the booklet's classification scale.

repair.proposal: Append further parts under the existing 'What does this mean?' instruction, using the same gym context: (a) r=0.64; (b) r=−0.64; (c) r=−0.90; (d) r=0.90. Add only: 'Predict what changes before answering each part.' Expected answers: moderate positive; moderate negative; strong negative; strong positive, with circumference tending to increase over time for positive coefficients and decrease for negative coefficients. Follow with the unpatterned part (e) r=−0.38. Answer: weak negative; circumference tends to decrease over time.

findings.doneWhen: Consecutive patterned parts change one feature at a time, followed by an unpatterned coefficient.
